EICMA 2026 • MTPeak Stole Some of the Spotlight at EICMA 2026 With Insane Power and Retro Looks on Three Wheels
These Designers Took a Crack at Building a Cargo E-Bike and Came Up With a Neat Utility Concept
14 photos
Photo: Tzu-How Chang | Eric Lee | FENG-YUE LEI | Nonnon YN Ho | An-Pin Chiu
Ah, the timeless bicycle, a vehicle that has been subject to so many spin-offs and approaches that we can write an entire book on the matter. With the arrival of electrification, this undying vehicle has gone under even more transformations.
Since stresses on e-bike frames are a bit different than on traditional ones, we’ve come to design bicycles differently these days. Some brands have even gone further and set their sights on the urban landscape, giving rise to wild frame designs that break the mold of what we’re used to. Dive even deeper, into let’s say, cargo bikes, and traditional frame cues go out the window.
Photo: Tzu-How Chang | Eric Lee | FENG-YUE LEI | Nonnon YN Ho | An-Pin Chiu For example, cargo e-bikes are available in two major styles, long tails, and long necks, as I like to call the latter. The former extends the rear of the bike in order to create a space where we can load up cargo, often, in the form of grocery baskets or seats and footrests for carrying children.
As for longnecks, they’re often denoted by an extended front end that places a large platform or basket at our disposal, and allowing for larger items. I’ve seen people carry other bikes on such a variation.
But, in between the lines of bicycle mechanics and styles, some brands and garage crews have explored some of the more obscure cues of design, giving rise to bikes that break the mold when compared to traditional ones.
Photo: Tzu-How Chang | Eric Lee | FENG-YUE LEI | Nonnon YN Ho | An-Pin Chiu Such a concept, exploration, or disruption of timeless styling and bicycle construction is called OUO, a two-wheeler aimed at the urban landscape and all about “utility.” Every single corner of the bike is aimed at doing something, so to speak, even calling upon a look that very few other bikes have been designed around.
For instance, the OUO is built with a U-shaped down tube that forms the head tube, BB, and seat tube. To help bring in some compliance or lateral strength, two top tubes connect the head tube, seat tube, and flow into the seat stay.
What I found rather neat about OUO is that the space between your legs, an area that is often left to no use, can be used for storing things like a laptop, some documents, or anything that can fit between those sidepanels.
Photo: Tzu-How Chang | Eric Lee | FENG-YUE LEI | Nonnon YN Ho | An-Pin Chiu More on the cargo side of things, the front and rear of the OUO are capable of carrying goodies. At the front, a tray is in place, a feature that’s spotted on quite the array of European bikes on the market, often, helping secure your essentials with the help of bungee cords, and at the rear, a classic pannier system is in place.
While the designers showcase no bags, we could easily add a couple and drape them over the sides of the rear wheel, as long as they don’t touch the ground; it appears as though 20-inch wheels are used for the OUO. It’s also not clear if this rack can support another person too, but probably can’t.
As for the rest of the bike, we don’t much about it as the ideation page makes no mention of what’s in store here, but what I found most interesting is that the minds and hands behind the OUO did take the concept all the way into a working concept.
Photo: Tzu-How Chang | Eric Lee | FENG-YUE LEI | Nonnon YN Ho | An-Pin Chiu There’s a little video below that shows it in action, and if I may, this means that the OUO is but a step away from production; the designers just need to secure a contract and sell the rights to a brand. Maybe they start it on their own.
While there are no details on the secondary gear of the OUO, we can see some of what’s in store. At the front, a suspension fork is in place, placing some bump-reducing action at our fingertips, but the rear is a stiff one, so we’ll be relying only on the cross-section of the tire to reduce vibrations.
In terms of electronics, a motor is spotted on the rear wheel, so it’s a hub-drive e-bike, and the battery pack, because the frame has no place to put it, is located on the seat tube, as it extends well into the saddle. It doesn’t look like the largest pack on the market, more like a range extender, but it should grant us access to at least 50 km of riding, maybe even more if it boasts more than 275 Wh of juice like most extenders.
Photo: Tzu-How Chang | Eric Lee | FENG-YUE LEI | Nonnon YN Ho | An-Pin Chiu Braking is handles by a pair of hydraulic clampers with four pistons each, granting us more stopping power than most e-bikes on the market, and if you ask me, essential for staying in control, especially with cargo on the bike.
Personally, I’m liking what the designers of OUO have done here, and if I may, for the right price, I’d bite. It’s compact, nimble, and actually looks decent for a twisted framework of pipes that break the mold of traditional bicycle design.
